summary:
American Samoa stands under the United States federal framework as an unorganised and unincorporated territory. Federal statutes and executive orders extend to it, while the territory's own code governs criminal law and marriage licensing. The criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy: the first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct, and the Fono's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether Obergefell v. Hodges reached the territory and said he did not know; the Governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article records that none has applied since.

The territory's judiciary has operated on the premise that the 2015 ruling does not automatically apply. In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told confirming senators, including retired High Court associate judge Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, that he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change. In July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment; as of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

The most recent dated authority, a 2026 article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa, concludes that Obergefell does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It sets out the litigation path: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Since 13 December 2022 the federal Respect for Marriage Act has obliged the territory to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change. The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties, referring instead to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

United States identity documents follow federal policy set in January 2025. An executive order requires passports to reflect sex assigned at birth, the 'X' marker available since 2022 has been eliminated, and new or renewed passports are processed only as M or F on supporting documents; passports already carrying an 'X' marker remain valid until expiration. The policy is challenged in federal courts, including a State Department suit filed by the ACLU on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad. Lambda Legal publishes guidance on which documents to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Three United States executive orders issued in 2025 reach the territory through federal agencies: measures defining sex as binary for federal documents and facilities and restricting healthcare funding, a further healthcare-funding measure, and a sports measure carrying a State Department visa restriction marked SWS25.

Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this inventory, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in Samoan scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend.
tangentialFactors:
In July 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. It remains, alongside several Indigenous self-governing jurisdictions, the only part of the United States enforcing a ban on same-sex couples marrying.

The 2003 bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not believe in marriages with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, and citing Christian upbringing. The hearing record therefore captures contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question rather than an outside characterisation.

The July 2024 survey by Dr Daniel Hall probed cultural dimensions alongside the constitutional question, including collectivistic versus individualistic orientation and linear versus polychronic time, on the premise that local culture bears on how a challenge would be judged.

The 2026 law-review article was written by two attorneys practising in American Samoa, one affiliated with American Samoa Legal Aid and working with the Freedom From Religion Foundation, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality of an untested licence application.

Sources describe the territory as tending toward tolerance and acceptance of transgender people and identities, as is the neighbouring independent state of Samoa, and identify the Samoan islands as the homeland of fa'afafine culture. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations in the same sources.

The 2025 federal measures are parent-nation instruments applied to the territory through federal agencies rather than local enactments, and the visa restriction attached to the sports measure carries the internal marking SWS25.

No outcome for the June 2023 action is stated.

For residents amending local records, the Office of Vital Statistics changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change, but the High Court of American Samoa's holding confines other alterations to errors present at recordation or to name changes on adoption.

Resident couples married lawfully outside the territory have been entitled to recognition and equal treatment under the federal Respect for Marriage Act since 13 December 2022, even though the territory does not perform such marriages.
